S1Result: If you plan to let Playwright's test agents write your tests, here is what ours cost.
Three agents wrote seven tests. It took forty six minutes. All seven pass.
So would you keep them? Here is what is good, and what to watch.
S2Setup: The planner explores the app and writes a test plan.
The generator turns the plan into test code, and checks every locator in a live browser.
The healer repairs tests that broke.
I ran them on a public demo app, and compared the result with six tests written in one pass, with no browser.
S3Numbers: The planner took under three minutes. The generator took forty three minutes.
The one pass suite has eighty lines of test code. The generated suite has two hundred and twenty three.
The one pass tests make about two and a half checks each. The generated tests make about nine.
S4Good: One page keeps hidden loading elements around. The generator saw them, and targeted the visible one.
The plan also told it to type into a disabled input. That step would hang.
The generator checked that the input is disabled instead.
S5Healer: Then the healer. I gave it a login test with six stale locators.
It repaired all six, in under two minutes.
But look at what came back. The stale ids came back as correct ids, not as role locators.
And it matched one button name with a leading space.
The healer repairs. It does not improve.
S6Verdict: So use the planner and the generator to scaffold tests for an app you do not know. Budget the time.
Review the checks. Nine per test is nine things to maintain.
Let the healer propose fixes in a pull request. Do not let it repair tests silently in your pipeline.
One caveat. This is one demo app, and one run. Measure on your own app.
S7EndCard: The tests, the plan and the numbers are in the public repo. The links are in the description.
